https://hungarytoday.hu/flydubai-restore.text: Flydubai Restores Budapest Service, with Daily Flights Planned for Winter Season Flydubai is resuming direct flights between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates. Starting July 31, the airline will once again operate flights from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Liszt Ferenc International Airport in Budapest (BUD). Initially offering three flights per week, the service will be expanded to daily flights with the winter schedule. The Dubai-based airline is strengthening its presence in Central and Eastern Europe. By resuming direct flights to Budapest, the airline is responding to sustained high demand, which has grown steadily since it first entered the Hungarian market in 2021. During the peak season, the reactivated route serves vacationers, business travelers, and the important VFR (visiting friends and relatives) traffic in equal measure. For flydubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith, the return to the Hungarian capital is a clear commitment to the market. “The resumption of flights underscores our long-term investment in Hungary and reflects the strong economic and cultural ties between the two nations. Budapest remains one of our most important strategic markets in Europe,” he explained. The renewed service not only offers travelers in the region more choice but also strengthens Dubai’s role as a global hub for business and tourism. Jeyhun Efendi, Senior Vice President of Commercial Operations at flydubai, is optimistic about the upcoming season. As we approach the busy fall-winter travel season, this flight connection creates valuable new trade and tourism opportunities in both markets,” he emphasized. For passengers from Hungary, the Dubai hub opens the door to the world. Dubai. Photo: flydubai Through the codeshare partnership with Emirates, travelers can seamlessly access flydubai’s global network with a single ticket and through-check baggage. This network now includes more than 120 destinations in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Southeast Asia—including popular long-haul destinations such as the Maldives, Thailand, Kenya, Sri Lanka, and Oman. The route will be served by a fleet of Boeing 737 aircraft. Passengers from Hungary will also benefit from flexible stopover options in Dubai, allowing them to explore the metropolis’s attractions, shopping districts, and family-friendly experiences. Photo: flydubai Flight operations will begin on July 31 with three weekly flights (Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays); starting October 25, 2026, the frequency will increase to one daily flight. The flight lands in Budapest at 9:40 p.m. and departs back to Dubai at 10:40 p.m. Fares from Budapest: Round-trip flights in Business Class starting at 802,400 forints (2,231 euros), in Economy Class starting at 182,900 forints (509 euros). Fares from Dubai: Round-trip flights in Business Class starting at 15,585 UAE dirhams (3,733 euros), in Economy Class starting at 2,987 UAE dirhams (715 euros). The flights are now available for booking via the airline’s official website, the airline’s official app, and through affiliated travel agencies and sales partners. Photo: flydubai Since its launch in June 2009, flydubai has become a major player in the region’s aviation industry. With a modern, uniform fleet of 97 Boeing 737s (including 68 Boeing 737 MAX 8s and 3 MAX 9s), the airline connects destinations in 58 countries. A key feature of its strategy remains the development of underserved markets. More than 100 routes have been launched to destinations that previously had no direct connection to Dubai. Since its founding, the airline has carried over 137 million passengers. The direct flight reduces travel time to about 4.5 hours. Beállítom Egy 44 éves férfi meghalt, a hétéves fiát pedig súlyos sérülésekkel kellett kórházba szállítani szombaton a szlovéniai Bohinj községben, a Savica-vízezésnél – írja a Delo.si a hegyimentők és a rendőrség közleménye alapján. Kettejük közül először a fiú zuhant szakadékba, az apja pedig a segítségére akart sietni, amikor maga is lezuhant. A család a magyar turisták között is népszerű Savica-vizeséshez (Száva-vízeséshez) kirándult el, majd onnan visszafelé sétálva egy, a turistaútnál lévő pihenőhelyen állt meg. A hétéves gyerek itt eltávolodott a családtagjaitól, majd a körülbelül 60 méter mély szurdokba zuhant. A fiú zuhanás közben elsikoltotta magát, amit a családtagjai meghallottak, az apja pedig azonnal utánaindult. A sikoltásokat követve kereste a fiút, majd maga is belezuhant a szurdokba. A bohinji hegyimentők erről szóló Facebook-posztja szerint azzal hívták őket, hogy „gyerek zuhant a szakadékba”. Mivel több egységük a környéken gyakorlatozott, azonnal el tudtak indulni a Savica-vízesés felé és néhány perccel később már ott is voltak. A hegyimentők kötelekkel ereszkedtek a körülbelül 60 méter mély szurdokmederbe, ahol a fiút élve, de súlyos sérülésekkel, az apját azonban már holtan találták meg. https://www.dw.com/en/trump-grants-visa-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Oupf Prefer DW on Google Zohran Mamdani said he spoke with President Donald Trump on Saturday Image: NDZ/STAR MAX/IPx/picture alliance Advertisement New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Saturday that US President Donald Trump had agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old boy who was killed in a neighborhood in Bronx earlier this week. Javits Frimpong moved to New York from Ghana last year to be with his father and begin a new life in the US, according to Representative Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx. Frimpong was shot in the abdomen on Thursday morning on his way to school and later died in the hospital, according to New York City police. There have been no arrests in the case so far, with police investigating the shooting. Mamdani says he spoke to Trump "I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately," Mamdani posted on X. "The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," he wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person." The killing led to an outpouring of grief in New York, with Torres writing, "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him." The White House is yet to respond to the news. Teen was bullied in school, father says Thomas Frimpong remembered his son as a quiet boy, and said he was bullied at school. Ghana's Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa thanked Mamdani and Trump in a post on X. He said Ghanaian officials were coordinating with Javits Frimpong's mother to assist her with the visa application process. Labor has introduced a bill to clarify obligations for lobbyist ‘guns for hire’. It has passed the lower house, though it may not become law before the election. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP New South Wales Analysis Icac’s drama and dirt files show NSW’s ‘guns for hire’ problem. But neither major party is serious about reform Anne Davies Chris Minns is trying to address the threat of undeclared lobbying but falls well short of what the commission recommended five years ago Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Thu 12 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Thu 12 Nov 2026 09.02 EST Share A dirt file on a state minister peddled to journalists. A subterranean campaign to discredit the building commissioner. Convincing the Liberal party to unseat councillors in the Hills district who were blocking a developer. The New South Wales corruption watchdog’s recent inquiry, Rosny, revealed the ease with which the key protagonists – a group of rightwing Liberal operatives known as the Reformers, all of whom were former staffers – could move along the corridors of NSW parliament. The Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) has alleged that, unbeknown to their fellow Liberals, the operatives – including the then treasurer, Dominic Perrottet’s own brother Charles Perrottet – were being paid $2m by one of NSW’s most notorious developers, Jean Nassif, and that they worked to progress his interests. Only one of the rightwing operatives involved in the Rosny inquiry was a registered lobbyist and subject to rules about declaring his clients and keeping records of interactions with ministers. Inside the group chats of the trash-talking NSW young Liberals who dreamed big – then imploded Read more Yet all of them were on first name terms with many of their former colleagues and bureaucrats, affording them easy access for a chin-wag or to mix with powerful players – especially within the Liberal party’s machine. Nassif – who told Icac he was “not corrupt” – has fled to Lebanon after the collapse of his company Toplace, leaving hundreds of buyers with substandard buildings. Charles Perrottet has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes. Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing. The issue of access for former staffers – whether they be third-party lobbyists employed by specialist lobbying firms who are “guns for hire”, or “government relations” specialists employed directly by companies or industry groups – has long been a concern for Icac. As Rosny showed, there was no way politicians could know who some of these figures were working for because these were allegedly undeclared guns for hire. The NSW Labor government has now introduced a bill to clarify obligations for at least one class of lobbyist: the guns for hire. It passed the lower house on Wednesday, though it may not become law before the election. Chris Minns’ efforts to address the threat that undeclared lobbying poses fall well short of what Icac recommended five years ago . First, the good bits of the proposed legislation. It would formally establish the NSW Electoral Commission as the regulator of third party lobbyists and bolster its investigative powers to audit compliance with the Lobbying of Government Officials Act and lobbyists code of conduct. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Icac recommended a separate lobbying commissioner but, given the electoral commission already has responsibility for the register, Minns has proposed it get the job. “Third-party lobbyists are already subject to information and disclosure obligations, including disclosing information to the electoral commission for publication on the lobbyists register,” the special minister of state, John Graham, told Guardian Australia. View image in fullscreen Screengrab of individuals questioned in Operation Rosny, an Icac investigation. Left to right, top row: Jean Nassif, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet. Bottom row: Damien Tudehope, Sharangan Maheswaran and Anita Perrottet. Composite: ICAC “The bill would allow the NSW Electoral Commission to audit compliance of third-party lobbyists and require relevant accounts, documents, information and explanations.” It also extends the act to third party lobbyists interacting with councils. Lobbyists interacting with councils will need to register and adhere to the code. This had been identified by Icac as a gap that needed fixing. But the bill also has bad bits. It ignores some of Icac’s most important recommendations. The most glaring loophole is that the disclosure regime doesn’t extend to staff employed directly by companies – usually with a title like “government relations” or “corporate affairs” – even through they also lobby politicians. How Icac turned into the ‘best show in town’ – Full Story podcast Read more These individuals make up about 80% of the people floating round the corridors of power. Most are former political staff members. Graham said registering in-house lobbyists would have “created unnecessary red tape given it is already clear whose interests are being served or represented, and ministerial diary disclosures provide transparency of lobbyists’ interaction”. This ignores the need for record keeping under the lobbyist regulations. If inhouse lobbyists were subject to the rules, they would be obliged to keep records of who they lobbied, as would the ministers and bureaucrats who were approached. The government argues it plans to enhance ministerial diary disclosures, to make them fully searchable, rather than issuing them quarterly in pdf form. The legislation will also clarify that third party lobbyists will need to disclose attendance at fundraising events involving exclusive or private access to a minister. But the bill does not extend to lobbyists’ interactions with key ministerial staff, such as their chief of staff – which Operation Rosny demonstrated were important conduits to the minister. “We’re regulating ministers and senior public servants because they’re decision makers. Ministerial staff are not decision makers,” Graham said. Chiefs of staff can be almost as powerful as their minister, because they control access – and can direct policy staff. Operation Rosny heard allegations about how the Liberal operatives, in their quest to smear the reputation of the building commissioner, provided material to a chief of staff, who then passed it to the chief of staff for the minister responsible for the building commissioner. The Liberal figures denied to Icac they were seeking to remove the building commissioner on behalf of Nassif. Icac also heard evidence that Charles Perrottet talked to ministers directly about the building commissioner. He was not a registered lobbyist, yet he enjoyed extraordinary access and influence. Neither the chiefs of staff nor the ministers were aware that Charles Perrottet was being paid by Nassif via a lobbying firm. The government has also watered down Icac’s proposals for a six-month prohibition on certain public service roles taking on lobbying roles in either lobbying firms or private enterprise when leaving the bureaucracy. Icac wanted certain sensitive roles to require six months’ “gardening leave” – as occurs when public servants leave the state’s gambling regulator. If the bill ever reaches the upper house – and its future is now uncertain – debate is likely to be feisty. The Greens have introduced a private member’s bill into parliament that would implement most of Icac’s recommendations from five years ago – including extending the lobbyists scheme to inhouse lobbyists. Kobi Shetty, the minor party’s anti-corruption spokesperson, said her bill would have included a four-year exclusion for some public sector employees. “When industries with deep pockets get a louder voice than the communities affected by their decisions, public trust in our democracy is eroded,” Shetty says. The Centre for Public Integrity senior counsel Geoffrey Watson says the government’s bill is a step in the right direction and he hopes it passes the Legislative Council. But he wishes the government had been more ambitious.
